344.title: Sleep: the bird returns to the tree (6.8)
344.hook: a bird on a string flies every way, finds no rest, and comes back to where it's tied; so does the mind, every night
344.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers use Uddalaka's tethered bird as an image for meditation on the breath, and the Upanishads' study of sleep, dream and deep sleep became a central theme in Vedanta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: food becomes mind, water becomes breath, heat becomes speech. The ember and the straw. Your line was you are what you eat, literally. Did you take a breath before a meal? Week three of year two begins. Day three hundred forty-four.
screen: `FOOD — YOU ARE WHAT YOU EAT, LITERALLY.`

segments.voice: Some nights your mind will not land. It's 1am and it's flying through tomorrow's meeting, last week's argument, a thing you said in seventh grade. Every direction, nowhere to rest. And then, at some point you never notice, it stops. You wake up and it's morning. Where did you go? Uddalaka has an answer, and he starts it with a pun, and then a picture of a bird on a string.
screen: `1AM, AND THE MIND WON'T LAND.` → `THEN, SOMEHOW, IT STOPS.` → `WHERE DID YOU GO?`

segments.voice: Learn from me about sleep, my dear, Uddalaka says. When a person sleeps, they become one with Being. They have gone to their own. And he plays on the Sanskrit. The word for he sleeps is svapiti. Uddalaka hears in it svam apita: gone to one's own. Sleep is going home. Then the picture. Imagine a bird tied by a string. It flies off this way, and that way, and every way, looking for somewhere else to rest, and finds nowhere. So in the end it settles down at the very place it's tied. The mind, he says, is just like that. It flies in every direction, finds no rest anywhere else, and settles down in the breath. For the mind, my dear, is tied to the breath. Think about what that means at 1am. All that flying is the bird pulling at the string, looking for rest out there, in plans and replays. Rest isn't out there. Rest is coming back to where you're tied: the breath, and, the Upanishad says, beneath the breath, Being itself. Then, at the end of this lesson, Uddalaka says for the very first time the three words he'll keep repeating to his son: tat tvam asi. You are that. We'll open those three words properly in a few days, with a handful of salt. For now, notice where the father chose to say them first: in a lesson about sleep. Every night, without trying, you go home. Rest is return.
screen: `SVAPITI: GONE TO ONE'S OWN.` · `A BIRD TIED BY A STRING.` · `THE MIND IS TIED TO THE BREATH.` · `TAT TVAM ASI, FOR THE FIRST TIME.` · then, large: `REST IS RETURN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice lets the bird come home. Sit or lie down, comfortably. Let the mind fly wherever it wants for a few breaths: plans, worries, memories. Don't stop it. Just watch it pull at the string. Then, gently, notice the breath, where the string is tied. Each time the mind flies off, let it come back and land on the next breath out. No effort. Just landing. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. In Uddalaka's teaching, going to one's own: the mind, like a tethered bird, comes to rest in the breath and in Being.
Your line: rest is return. Tonight, when your mind starts flying, picture the bird on its string, and let it come back to one breath. Day three hundred forty-four.

345.title: The bees and the honey — no juice says "I am from this tree" (6.9)
345.hook: bees gather nectar from many different trees, and in the honey, no drop can say which tree it came from
345.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often take Uddalaka's lessons one at a time, as here, and the honey image is one of several the Chandogya uses for creatures merging into Being in sleep and death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleep, the bird on a string that comes back to where it's tied. Your line was rest is return. Did your mind land on one breath last night? Day three hundred forty-five.

Pick up a jar of honey. Wildflower, the label says. That means bees went out and visited clover, and dandelion, and an apple tree, and a lime tree, and plenty of other flowers no one will ever list. They brought it all home and worked it together, and now it's one golden thing in a jar. Try to find the apple-tree part. You can't. It's not that it's gone. It's in there. It just can't be picked out anymore. Uddalaka, teaching his son, picks up the same jar.
screen: `WILDFLOWER HONEY.` → `CLOVER, DANDELION, APPLE, LIME.` → `FIND THE APPLE-TREE PART.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: just as bees make honey, my dear, by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing them to a single sweetness, and in the honey those juices can't tell one another, I am the juice of this tree, I am the juice of that tree, in the same way, all these creatures, when they merge into Being, in deep sleep and at death, don't know: we have merged into Being. They don't keep their labels. Then he adds a line that's easy to skip, and shouldn't be. Whatever they are in this world, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, they become that again. So the honey isn't the end of the story. Each one comes back as itself. Hold both halves. In the depth of Being, in the honey, the separate names are gone. And here, in the world, the tiger wakes up a tiger and the mosquito a mosquito. So Uddalaka isn't erasing anyone's life. In his picture, underneath a name, a family, a whole history, there is one sweetness shared with everything that lives. And from the inside, he says, no one notices the merging. No juice says, I've merged. A person sleeps, wakes up, and goes back to being themselves. Then, once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that, Shvetaketu. Please, sir, says the son, tell me more.

segments.voice: Today's practice tastes the honey. Sit and settle. Listen to the room. Pick out the separate sounds one at a time: a fan, a car outside, a voice somewhere, your own breath. Name each one. Then, breath by breath, stop naming them and let them run together into one sound, the way the juices run together in the honey, no part saying where it came from. Rest in that one sound for a while. The bell holds the time.
Madhu, honey, sweetness. Many juices, one sweetness: in Being, no creature says I came from this tree, and in the world, each comes back as itself.

Your line: the rivers lose their names, just as the juices lose their trees. Today, notice one place where many separate things become one: a crowd, a choir, a shared meal. Day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: The rivers and the sea (6.10)
346.hook: rivers run east and west, each with its own name, and in the sea not one of them can say 'I am this river'
346.tomorrow: the tree: cut it, it bleeds
346.howItsDone: Rivers are sacred for many Hindus, who bathe in them on festival days and immerse ashes after cremation; Vedanta teachers often use Uddalaka's rivers and the sea to describe the relation of the self to Brahman.

segments.voice: Yesterday: madhu, many juices, one sweetness. Your line was the rivers lose their names. Today we meet those rivers. Where did you see many become one? Day three hundred forty-six.

Rivers have names, and people love those names. They write songs about them, fight over them, scatter ashes in them, bathe in them on holy days. The Ganga, the Yamuna, the Mississippi, the Thames. A river has a source, a path, a personality: slow and brown, or fast and cold. And then a river reaches the sea. Stand on a beach and look out. Which part of that water was the Ganga? Uddalaka asks his son the same thing.
screen: `RIVERS HAVE NAMES.` → `SONGS, ASHES, HOLY DAYS.` → `WHICH PART WAS THE GANGA?`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: these rivers, my dear, the eastern ones flow toward the east, the western ones toward the west. They go from sea to sea. They become the sea itself. And there, in the sea, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one. Notice the little phrase, from sea to sea. Commentators hear the water cycle in it: water rises from the sea as cloud, falls as rain, gathers into rivers, and runs back home. The river was the sea all along, on a long walk. Then he turns it around. In the same way, my dear, all these creatures, though they have come from Being, don't know: we have come from Being. Yesterday's honey was about going in and losing the label. Today is about coming out and forgetting the source. A river in the mountains doesn't feel like the ocean. It feels like a river: narrow, rushing, very much itself. A person can feel like that too: a particular someone, in a particular bed, with particular worries. And Uddalaka says again, whatever they are here, tiger or lion or gnat, they become that. The river is truly a river while it runs. He doesn't erase it. He only points out where it comes from and where it goes. Then the refrain, once more: that subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. You are that, Shvetaketu. Some Vedanta schools hear the river as finally nothing but sea. Others hear the river as a real, beloved part of the sea.
screen: `EAST AND WEST, FROM SEA TO SEA.` · `THEY DON'T KNOW: I AM THIS RIVER.` · `THEY DON'T KNOW WHERE THEY CAME FROM.` · `THE RIVER IS TRULY A RIVER.` · then, large: `THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice follows a river home. Sit and settle. Picture a river you know, or one you've seen in pictures. Start at its source, a spring in the hills. On each breath, let it run a little farther: past towns, under bridges, wider and slower. Then let it reach the sea. Watch the edge where river becomes ocean. Then rest there, in the open water, without needing to know which part was which. The bell holds the time.
Samudra, the sea, the gathering of waters. Rivers flow from sea to sea, become the sea, and there don't say I am this river; so creatures come from Being and don't know it.
Your line: the sea. Today, in a crowd or on a busy street, notice how many separate lives are flowing the same way, each one still itself. Day three hundred forty-six.

347.title: The tree — cut it, it bleeds; leave it, it lives (6.11)
347.hook: strike a great tree at the root and sap runs out, but it lives; when life leaves a branch, the branch dries up
347.howItsDone: At Hindu deathbeds and funerals, families may recite or reflect on scriptures that teach that the self does not die with the body, from the Upanishads to the Bhagavad Gita's second chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samudra, from sea to sea, not knowing I am this river. Your line was the sea. Did a glass of water remind you? Day three hundred forty-seven.

Find an old tree with a scar on it: a place where a branch was cut, or a car hit it, or someone carved initials years ago. Often you'll see where the sap ran, dried now into a hard, shiny crust. The tree bled. And it's still standing, still leafing out every spring. Next to it, maybe, there's one branch that's gray and bare, that never came back. Same tree. One part alive, one part not. Uddalaka points his son to a great tree.
screen: `AN OLD TREE WITH A SCAR.` → `IT BLED, AND IT'S STILL STANDING.` → `ONE GRAY BRANCH.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: my dear, if someone were to strike this great tree at its root, it would bleed sap, but it would live. Strike it in the middle, it would bleed, but live. Strike it at the top, it would bleed, but live. Filled through and through by the living self, it stands, drinking in water, rejoicing. Then: if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If it leaves a second, that one dries up. If it leaves a third, that dries up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. And then the line that turns it toward his son. In the same way, my dear, understand this: the body dies when life leaves it. But life does not die. Notice the order of the lesson. First, life is everywhere in the tree: root, middle, top. You can wound it in any of those places and it carries on, because life isn't sitting in one spot that you could cut out. It pervades. Second, the body depends on life, not the other way around. A dry branch isn't the death of life. It's life leaving that branch. For Uddalaka, the same is true of us. The body is a tree. Something fills it, makes it drink and grow and rejoice, and when that something leaves, the body falls. But what left doesn't fall with it. And once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this. You are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `STRIKE IT: IT BLEEDS, BUT LIVES.` · `DRINKING IN WATER, REJOICING.` · `LIFE LEAVES A BRANCH; IT DRIES.` · `THE BODY DIES. LIFE DOES NOT.` · then, large: `LIFE PERVADES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice feels the life in the tree. Sit and settle. Bring your attention to your feet, your roots. Feel that something is alive there: warmth, tingling, pulse. Move up to your middle: belly, chest, the breath moving. Then to your top: face, scalp. The same life, root to crown. Rest in it, the way the tree stands drinking in water, rejoicing. The bell holds the time.
The tree. Uddalaka's great tree, filled by the living self: wounded, it lives; when life leaves, it dries; the body dies, but life does not.
Your line: life pervades. Today, stop by one tree or plant for a moment, and notice that it is drinking, growing, alive in every part. Day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: The banyan seed — "break it. what do you see? nothing. from that nothing, this tree"…
348.hook: the father has his son split a banyan fig, then a seed inside it, and asks what he sees: nothing at all
348.howItsDone: The banyan is sacred to many Hindus and is often worshipped, especially by women during the Vat Savitri festival; teachers use Uddalaka's banyan seed to explain the subtle essence behind the visible world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tree, struck at root, middle and top, bleeding but alive. Your line was life pervades. Did you stop by a tree or a plant? Day three hundred forty-eight.

A banyan doesn't stop at one trunk. It sends roots down from its branches, and those roots thicken into new trunks, until one tree can look like a small forest. Birds nest in it, and people sit in its shade, and all of it is one tree. Its fruit is a little fig a bird could swallow whole, and inside are seeds like specks of dust. Uddalaka sends his son to fetch one of those figs.
screen: `A TREE THAT LOOKS LIKE A FOREST.` → `ROOTS THAT BECOME TRUNKS.` → `IT STARTED AS A TINY SEED.`

segments.voice: The lesson is a short conversation, almost a game. Bring me a fruit from that banyan. Here it is, sir. Break it. It's broken, sir. What do you see? These tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them. It's broken, sir. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir. And then the father says: my dear, that subtle essence you can't see, from that very essence this great banyan tree stands. Believe me, my dear. Notice how he teaches. He doesn't describe the seed. He has his son break it with his own hands and look. And the son reports honestly: nothing. That nothing is the point. Not empty nothing. Too-fine-to-see nothing. The Sanskrit word Uddalaka uses is anima, the subtlest, the finest. The whole enormous tree, trunks and roots and shade and birds, rests on something so fine it can't be seen at all. And then he asks for something we haven't heard him ask before: shraddhatsva, believe me, have faith. He isn't asking his son to believe without looking. He's just had him look as hard as anyone can. One way to hear it: when looking runs out, at the edge of what can be seen, don't conclude there's nothing there. The tree is standing right in front of you. Then the refrain, once more: that subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. You are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` · `WHAT DO YOU SEE? NOTHING AT ALL.` · `ANIMA: THE SUBTLEST.` · `SHRADDHATSVA: BELIEVE ME, MY DEAR.` · then, large: `FROM THAT, THIS GREAT TREE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks for what can't be seen. Sit and settle. Notice something big in your life: your body, your family, your work. Then go smaller, the way Uddalaka had his son break the fruit and then the seed. What's this made of? And that? Keep going, breath by breath, until you reach a place where you can't see any further. Don't force an answer. Rest at the edge of what you can see. The bell holds the time.
Anima, the subtlest, the finest. Broken open, the banyan seed shows nothing at all; from that unseen, subtle essence, the father says, the great banyan stands.
Your line: the subtle essence. Today, notice one big thing that started from something tiny: a habit, a friendship, an idea, a tree on your street. Day three hundred forty-eight.

349.title: The salt in water — "taste it here. here. everywhere." (6.13)
349.hook: drop salt in water overnight; in the morning you can't find it, but sip from any side and it's there
349.carry: tat tvam asi — you are that
349.howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is one of the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, and in some traditions it is taught to monks at their initiation; each Vedanta school has its own commentary on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anima, broken open, and nothing at all inside. Your line was the subtle essence. What big thing did you trace back to something tiny? Day three hundred forty-nine.

You can try this one tonight. Take a glass of water and a pinch of salt. Drop the salt in. Watch it for a moment: the grains sink, cloud, and then disappear. Leave it overnight. In the morning, try to pick the salt back out. You can't. It isn't anywhere you can point to. And yet, you know it's in there. You know exactly how to find out. This is Uddalaka's most famous lesson, and the one where his three-word refrain finally lands with full weight.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER, A PINCH OF SALT.` → `IN THE MORNING, PICK IT OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T. BUT IT'S THERE.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: put this salt in water, and come to me in the morning. Shvetaketu does. In the morning his father says: bring me the salt you put in last night. He looks, and can't find it, because it has dissolved. Then: sip from this end. How is it? Salty. Sip from the middle. How is it? Salty. Sip from the far end. How is it? Salty. Then, the father says, you don't see Being here, my dear, but it is truly here. That subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. Tat tvam asi, Shvetaketu. You are that. Those three words are among the most famous in all of Hindu scripture. Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are. Later teachers counted them among the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, of the Upanishads. Here's what the salt adds. The honey and the rivers showed the names dissolving. The seed showed the essence too fine to see. The salt shows it's everywhere at once. Not hiding in one spot. Not a ghost in a corner. Every sip, every drop. And the schools of Vedanta hear the three words differently. Shankara's Advaita hears pure identity: your deepest self and Being are one. Ramanuja hears the self as real and distinct, yet belonging to Brahman, the way a body belongs to its soul. Madhva's Dvaita school reads the same Sanskrit with a different word break, as atat tvam asi: you are not that, not the same as the Lord. Each school has a long tradition of teachers behind it. All of them taste the same water.

segments.voice: Today's practice tastes for the salt. Sit and settle. Notice your hands: is there awareness here? Yes. Your feet: is it here too? Yes. Your breath: here? Yes. A sound in the room: here as well. Like sipping from one end, the middle, the far end. Don't look for anything special. Just notice that the same plain awareness is in every place you check. Rest in that. If you'd like, let the three words sound once in your mind: tat tvam asi. The bell holds the time.
The salt in water. Dissolved, it can't be picked out, yet every sip is salty: Being is unseen, and truly here.
Your line: tat tvam asi. You are that. Tonight, if you'd like, try the salt in a glass of water, and taste it in the morning. Day three hundred forty-nine.

350.title: The blindfolded man led home (6.14)
350.hook: a man is led away blindfolded and left in the wilderness; someone unties him and points, and he asks his way home, village by village

350.howItsDone: Hindu traditions give the guru, the teacher, a place of honor, and many communities observe Guru Purnima each year to give thanks to their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the salt in water, salty, salty, salty. Your line was tat tvam asi, you are that. Did you taste the water in the morning? Today ends week three of year two. Day three hundred fifty.
screen: `THE SALT IN WATER — TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Shvetaketu has heard about honey and rivers, trees and seeds and salt. And still, maybe, he's thinking what anyone would think. Fine. Being is everywhere, and I am that. So why don't I feel it? Why am I still lost? His father doesn't scold him, and he doesn't repeat the salt one more time. He tells him about a man led far from home with a cloth tied over his eyes.
screen: `HONEY, RIVERS, TREES, SEEDS, SALT.` → `SO WHY DON'T I FEEL IT?` → `A MAN WITH A CLOTH OVER HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: Suppose, Uddalaka says, someone leads a man away from his home in Gandhara with his eyes covered, and leaves him in a lonely, empty place. The man turns and shouts, east, north, south: I was brought here blindfolded and left here blindfolded! Then someone comes along, unties the cloth, and says: Gandhara is that way. Go. And the man, asking from village to village, informed and thinking for himself, gets all the way home. In the same way, Uddalaka says, a person who has a teacher knows. Notice who does what. The stranger doesn't carry the man home. He takes off the blindfold and points. The man still has to walk, and ask, and use his own head, village after village. A teacher, in this picture, isn't a taxi. A teacher is someone who points. And notice what the man lacked. Not legs, not a road. Gandhara was there the whole time. He just couldn't see which way to turn. Uddalaka adds that, for such a person, the only delay is until he's released from the body; then he arrives. And the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu. This week, in order. Sleep, the bird coming back to where it's tied. The honey, where no juice knows its tree. Samudra. The tree that bleeds and lives. Anima, and nothing inside. The salt in water. And today, the blindfold untied. Seven lessons, one teaching, and a father pointing the way.
screen: `BLINDFOLDED AND LEFT ALONE.` · `SOMEONE UNTIES IT AND POINTS.` · `HE ASKS, VILLAGE BY VILLAGE.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `ONE WITH A TEACHER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice remembers who pointed. Sit and settle. Think of someone who untied a blindfold for you: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, someone who said one sentence that turned you around. See their face. Remember what they said or did. Notice that they didn't walk the road for you. They pointed, and you walked. Let gratitude rise, if it's there. The bell holds the time.
Acharyavan, one who has a teacher. Untied and pointed toward Gandhara, he asks his way village by village; so one who has a teacher knows.
Your line: someone points the way. Today, thank one person who once pointed you in a direction, with a message, a call, or a word. Day three hundred fifty.
